summary: Defines IANA registries for W3C Web Authentication attestation statement format identifiers and extension identifiers.

eli5.summary: A list kept in one place so that different login-by-key systems use the same names for their features.

questions: where are webauthn attestation formats registered
how do i register a webauthn format
subtitle: Official IANA registries for WebAuthn features.

tldr.problem: Web Authentication (WebAuthn), a W3C standard for passwordless login with hardware keys, has pluggable components—different kinds of attestation formats and extensions. These need coordinated names across the ecosystem.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC establishes two IANA registries: one for attestation statement format identifiers and one for extension identifiers. Both use Specification Required registration with designated expert review.
tldr.outcome: WebAuthn implementers can now register new formats and extensions through a stable, open IANA registry, ensuring interoperability.

today: RFC 8809 defines the registries as they stand today. Both the Attestation Statement Format Identifiers and Extension Identifiers registries at IANA are managed according to this RFC's procedures, with designated experts reviewing new proposals.

sections.title: What Is WebAuthn?
sections.content:
Web Authentication (WebAuthn) is a W3C web standard that lets websites authenticate users by verifying possession of a cryptographic key, such as a hardware security key or a device's biometric fingerprint. Unlike passwords, a WebAuthn credential is specific to the website and cannot be stolen or phished as easily.

WebAuthn allows for different methods of attesting (proving) that a key is genuine, called attestation statement formats. It also allows optional extensions to add extra features—such as user verification hints or custom data. For an ecosystem to function, these pluggable components need registered, agreed-upon identifiers so that a client and server can recognize the same attestation format or extension.
sections.eli5: WebAuthn is a way to log into websites using a hardware key or your phone instead of a password. New features are added over time. This creates official lists so every company knows what to call each feature.

sections.title: Attestation Statement Format Identifiers
sections.content:
An attestation statement is proof that a key is genuine—that it comes from a real hardware key or device, not a fake. Different types of keys produce attestations in different formats. For instance, a FIDO2 security key might produce one format, while an Apple device might produce another.

The RFC establishes an IANA registry for these format identifiers. Each entry must be a string of 32 octets or less, using printable ASCII characters only. Format identifiers are case-sensitive and must be unique. New formats are registered using the "Specification Required" policy—meaning a freely available, stable specification must accompany the request and be reviewed by designated experts.

Initial entries in the registry come from the W3C WebAuthn specification itself. The W3C Web Authentication Working Group is named as the change controller, meaning they manage updates to those core formats.
sections.eli5: Different keys prove themselves in different ways. This registry lists all the official ways and what to call them, so everyone's software recognizes them.

sections.title: Extension Identifiers
sections.content:
WebAuthn is designed to be extensible. Extensions allow the WebAuthn protocol to be enhanced with optional features without breaking existing implementations. For example, an extension might request that the authenticator verify the user's identity with a PIN or fingerprint, or might ask for custom data to be signed along with the normal WebAuthn response.

Like attestation formats, extensions need registered identifiers. The RFC establishes a second IANA registry for extension identifiers with the same rules: 32 octets or less, printable ASCII, case-sensitive, and unique. Registration uses the "Specification Required" policy with expert review. Initial entries come from the W3C WebAuthn specification, with the W3C Web Authentication Working Group as the change controller.
sections.eli5: Extensions are extra features that websites can ask for. This registry lists all the official extensions and what to call them.

sections.title: How to Register New Formats and Extensions
sections.content:
A vendor or researcher who develops a new attestation format or extension can request registration by providing a brief description, a reference to a freely available, stable specification that includes security and privacy considerations, and naming a change controller (the responsible party who will maintain the entry). The request goes to the webauthn-reg-review@ietf.org mailing list.

Designated experts (appointed and maintained by the IETF and the WebAuthn community) review the request for completeness and technical soundness. They may refuse a request if it is incompletely specified or if it raises security or privacy concerns. When approved, IANA processes the registration. The IESG acts as a final arbiter for objections.

As a special accommodation, an expert may register an unregistered but widely-deployed format or extension if the original developer is not registering it themselves and timely registration seems unlikely.
sections.eli5: If you create a new feature for WebAuthn, you can officially register it by writing a specification and asking the experts. They check that it is safe and makes sense, then add it to the list.
